pos: n. pl. (lightning strokes accompanied by thunder)
etymology: From thunder, Old English thunor, and bolt, Old English bolt, an arrow or missile. The Hebrew word reshephim means flames or fiery bolts.
biblical_def: Psalm 78 rehearses God's mighty works in Egypt so that Israel's children would not forget them. Among the plagues it recalls the hail: “He gave up their cattle also to the hail, and their flocks to hot thunderbolts.” Exodus records that the LORD sent thunder and hail, and the fire ran along upon the ground, so that there was hail and fire mingled with the hail, very grievous, such as there was none like it in all the land of Egypt since it became a nation (Exodus 9:23-24). The psalm presents the plagues not as natural disasters but as personal judgments of the God who “cast upon them the fierceness of his anger” (Psalm 78:49). The thunderbolts fell on Egypt's flocks while the land of Goshen was spared. The psalmist's purpose was pastoral: to teach the next generation that they might set their hope in God and not forget His works (78:7). The God who commands the lightning is the same God who redeemed His people. The thunder that terrified Egypt is a sign of His power over creation, and of the certainty of His judgment on all who harden their hearts against Him as Pharaoh did.

corruption_summary: The plagues are explained away as a chain of natural phenomena, stripping the thunderbolts of their character as the personal judgment of the LORD on Egypt.
corruption_paragraphs: Naturalistic accounts of the exodus treat the plagues as a sequence of ecological events, a red tide, frogs, insects, a volcanic storm, with nothing supernatural in them. That reading cannot explain the timing at Moses' word, the sparing of Goshen, or the death of the firstborn, and it contradicts the psalm's plain claim that God Himself sent them.

Scripture presents the God who controls the weather as Lord of creation and Judge of nations. The thunderbolts on Egypt were His acts, done to make His name known and to redeem His people. Psalm 78 calls every generation to remember them and to set their hope in God.

pos: n. pl. (stones hurled from a sling)
etymology: A compound of sling, from Middle English slyngen, to fling, and stone, from Old English stan. The Hebrew is literally stones of the sling.
biblical_def: In the LORD's answer to Job out of the whirlwind, He describes leviathan, a creature no man can master: “The arrow cannot make him flee: slingstones are turned with him into stubble.” Every weapon of the ancient warrior is listed and found useless: sword, spear, dart, habergeon, arrow, slingstones and darts are all counted as stubble against him (Job 41:26-29). The purpose of the description is not zoology but humility. “None is so fierce that dare stir him up: who then is able to stand before me?” (Job 41:10). If man cannot stand before a creature God has made, how can he contend with the Creator? Job had demanded that God answer him; God's answer was to show Job his smallness, and Job responded, “I abhor myself, and repent in dust and ashes” (Job 42:6). The slingstone was the weapon David used to slay Goliath, but in David's case the stone succeeded because the battle was the LORD's. Human weapons are stubble unless God gives the victory; against Him they are stubble always.

webster_full: SLING, n. An instrument for throwing stones, consisting of a strap and two strings.
SLINGSTONE, n. A stone thrown or to be thrown by a sling.
Job 41:28 says slingstones are turned into stubble against leviathan.

corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The word is simply archaic.

Modern man trusts his technology as the ancients trusted their slings and swords. Job 41 humbles that confidence. Creation itself holds powers beyond human mastery, and the God who made them is infinitely greater. The fitting response is Job's: to lay the hand upon the mouth and repent.

etymology: From Middle English hurlen, probably imitative or related to Low German hurreln, to toss. The Hebrew word means to cast or throw.
biblical_def: The law of the cities of refuge carefully distinguished murder from accidental killing. Among the marks of murder: “But if he thrust him of hatred, or hurl at him by laying of wait, that he die;” then “he that smote him shall surely be put to death; for he is a murderer” (Numbers 35:21). Hatred, ambush and a weapon hurled with intent marked the deed as wilful. By contrast, the man who killed “without enmity” or cast a stone “seeing him not” (35:22-23) could flee to a city of refuge and be safe from the avenger of blood. The law thus looked at the heart behind the hand. God values human life because man is made in His image (Genesis 9:6), and He requires that deliberate murder be punished by the magistrate; yet He also protects the one who kills without malice. Christ deepened the same principle when He taught that hatred itself is murder in the heart (Matthew 5:21-22; 1 John 3:15). The cities of refuge also point to Christ, the refuge to whom guilty sinners flee and in whom they are safe from the avenger.

webster_full: HURL, v.t. To send or drive with violence; to throw with violence; as, to hurl a stone or dart.
To utter with vehemence; as, to hurl defiance.

corruption_summary: Modern justice often ignores the moral weight of intent or abandons the biblical principle that wilful murder deserves the magistrate's gravest sentence.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The verb keeps its plain sense.

The principle to recover is the law's careful distinction between malice and accident, and its high view of human life as bearing God's image. Scripture grounds the magistrate's sword in Genesis 9:6 and Romans 13:4, and it judges hatred as murder of the heart. Both civil justice and personal holiness are shaped by it.

etymology: From Middle Dutch rover, a robber, from roven, to rob. The Hebrew gedud means a troop or raiding band.
biblical_def: The Chronicler lists the mighty men who came to David at Ziklag while he was still a fugitive from Saul. Some of Manasseh joined him, “And they helped David against the band of the rovers: for they were all mighty men of valour, and were captains in the host.” The band of the rovers is the Amalekite raiding party that burned Ziklag and carried away the wives and children of David's men (1 Samuel 30:1-2). In that dark hour David's own men spoke of stoning him, “but David encouraged himself in the LORD his God” (1 Samuel 30:6), enquired of the LORD, pursued the raiders and recovered all. The Chronicler adds that loyal men came to David day by day to help him, “until it was a great host, like the host of God” (1 Chronicles 12:22). The rovers stand for every enemy that plunders the camp of God's anointed while he is in distress. The lesson is that God gathers help to His chosen king, and that the Son of David will likewise recover all that the enemy has carried away.

webster_full: ROVER, n. A wanderer; one who rambles about.

corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The word survives in its general sense of a wanderer.

The account rewards meditation. When the rovers had stripped Ziklag, David strengthened himself in the LORD and recovered all, and God sent mighty men to stand with him. Believers who suffer loss in the service of Christ may take heart: the greater Son of David will recover all His own.

etymology: From Old French rifler, to scratch, strip or plunder. The Hebrew word means to plunder or spoil.
biblical_def: Zechariah's final vision begins with the darkest picture of Jerusalem's distress: “For I will gather all nations against Jerusalem to battle; and the city shall be taken, and the houses rifled, and the women ravished; and half of the city shall go forth into captivity, and the residue of the people shall not be cut off from the city.” Houses ransacked, women violated, half the city led away: the LORD Himself gathers the nations for this judgment. Yet the very next verse turns the tide: “Then shall the LORD go forth, and fight against those nations, as when he fought in the day of battle” (Zechariah 14:3). His feet stand upon the mount of Olives, and “the LORD shall be king over all the earth: in that day shall there be one LORD, and his name one” (14:9). Interpreters differ on the details of this chapter, but its message is plain: God's people pass through severe tribulation, a remnant is preserved, and the LORD Himself comes to deliver and to reign. The rifled houses of Jerusalem are not the end of the story; the end is a city where every pot is holiness to the LORD of hosts.

corruption_paragraphs: Zechariah 14 is a favourite text of dispensational prophecy charts, which read it as a literal battle plan for a future war centred on the modern state of Israel. That system, a nineteenth-century novelty, subordinates the New Testament's interpretation of the prophets to newspaper speculation.

Reformed interpreters read the chapter in the light of Christ and His kingdom. However its details are understood, its message is sure: the people of God suffer, the LORD preserves a remnant, and He comes to reign over all the earth. The rifled city becomes the holy city.

etymology: From un-, not, and taken, from Old Norse taka, to take. In 2 Corinthians 3:14 it renders a Greek phrase meaning not unveiled or not lifted.
biblical_def: Paul contrasts the ministry of Moses with the ministry of the Spirit. When Moses came down from the mount his face shone, and he put a vail over it. Paul applies the vail to Israel's heart: “But their minds were blinded: for until this day remaineth the same vail untaken away in the reading of the old testament; which vail is done away in Christ.” The Jews of Paul's day read Moses every sabbath, yet did not see that he wrote of Christ. The problem was not in the text but in the reader; a vail lay upon the heart. That vail is removed only in Christ: “Nevertheless when it shall turn to the Lord, the vail shall be taken away” (2 Corinthians 3:16). This is the key to reading the whole Bible. The Old Testament is not a separate religion but the promise of which Christ is the fulfilment, and without Him it remains a vailed book. With Him, believers “beholding as in a glass the glory of the Lord, are changed into the same image from glory to glory” (3:18). Only the Spirit of God removes the vail, which is why conversion and right understanding of Scripture always go together.

corruption_summary: The Old Testament is read apart from Christ, whether by critics who treat it as Israel's evolving religion or by preachers who moralize its stories, leaving the vail untaken away.
corruption_paragraphs: Historical-critical scholarship reads the Old Testament as a record of Israel's developing religious ideas with no organic connection to Christ. Many evangelical sermons, though orthodox, reduce its narratives to moral lessons about courage or obedience. In both cases the vail remains.

Christ taught that Moses and all the prophets wrote of Him (Luke 24:27). The Reformed tradition reads Scripture as one covenant story fulfilled in Christ. To read the Old Testament rightly is to read it with the vail taken away, beholding His glory in every page.

etymology: From Old French forcible, from force, from Late Latin fortia, strength, from fortis, strong. The Hebrew word means to be strong or sharp, even grievous.
biblical_def: Job's friends had come to comfort him and stayed to accuse him. Wearied by their speeches, Job answered: “How forcible are right words! but what doth your arguing reprove?” Job did not object to correction; he had just said, “Teach me, and I will hold my tongue: and cause me to understand wherein I have erred” (Job 6:24). What he objected to was arguing that missed the mark. Right words are forcible: they strike home, they carry their own weight, they need no padding. His friends' arguments, however eloquent, did not reprove him because they were not right; they applied true principles falsely to his case. The verse teaches the power of truth rightly spoken. God's own Word is the supreme example: “For the word of God is quick, and powerful, and sharper than any twoedged sword” (Hebrews 4:12). Counsellors, preachers and parents should aim not at many words but at right words, fitly spoken, which are like apples of gold in pictures of silver (Proverbs 25:11).

Job's complaint warns all who counsel the suffering. His friends spoke many true things about God's justice, but applied them falsely and without compassion. Right words are forcible because they are true and fitly applied; the church's counsel must be both biblically sound and rightly fitted to the case.

etymology: From un-, not, and occupied, from Old French occuper, from Latin occupare, to seize or take possession of. The Hebrew says the highways ceased.
biblical_def: The Song of Deborah describes Israel's condition under Canaanite oppression: “In the days of Shamgar the son of Anath, in the days of Jael, the highways were unoccupied, and the travellers walked through byways.” The main roads were too dangerous to use; travellers crept along crooked paths to avoid the enemy. Village life ceased, “until that I Deborah arose, that I arose a mother in Israel” (Judges 5:7). The cause of the desolation is named in the next verse: “They chose new gods; then was war in the gates” (Judges 5:8). Unoccupied highways were the outward sign of a deeper apostasy. When Israel forsook the LORD, He gave them into the hand of Jabin king of Canaan, and the land fell into fear. When they cried to Him, He raised up deliverers. The song celebrates God's victory through Deborah, Barak and Jael, and ends, “So let all thine enemies perish, O LORD: but let them that love him be as the sun when he goeth forth in his might” (Judges 5:31). The deserted roads of Judges remind every generation that national security flows from national faithfulness.

Judges traces the cycle plainly: Israel chose new gods, and war came to the gates. Modern nations explain disorder by economics and politics alone, but Scripture names apostasy as the deeper cause. The remedy is repentance and return to the LORD, who raises up deliverers for His people.

etymology: From un-, not, and accustomed, from Old French acostumer, from costume, custom, from Latin consuetudo. The Hebrew says not taught or not trained.
biblical_def: Jeremiah records the lament of Ephraim, the northern tribes, in their exile: “I have surely heard Ephraim bemoaning himself thus; Thou hast chastised me, and I was chastised, as a bullock unaccustomed to the yoke: turn thou me, and I shall be turned; for thou art the LORD my God.” An untrained bullock kicks against the yoke and must be broken to it; so Ephraim had resisted God's discipline. But now the chastisement has done its work, and Ephraim prays one of the great prayers of Scripture: “Turn thou me, and I shall be turned.” Ephraim knows that repentance is God's gift; he cannot turn himself. And God responds with tender mercy: “Is Ephraim my dear son? is he a pleasant child? ... my bowels are troubled for him; I will surely have mercy upon him, saith the LORD” (Jeremiah 31:20). The verse stands just before the promise of the new covenant (31:31-34). It teaches that God's chastening of His children is fatherly, that its aim is their turning, and that the turning itself is His sovereign grace.

corruption_summary: Repentance is treated as a human decision man can make at will, when Ephraim's prayer confesses that the sinner turns only when God turns him.
corruption_paragraphs: Arminian and Pelagian theologies make repentance the sinner's own act, done in the strength of a free will that God merely invites. Ephraim's prayer contradicts it: the bullock does not break itself to the yoke, and the sinner does not turn himself. Turn thou me, and I shall be turned.

The 1689 Confession teaches that repentance unto life is an evangelical grace (15.1), wrought by the Spirit in effectual calling. God's chastening is the means; His mercy is the cause. Believers who resist His discipline should pray as Ephraim prayed, confident that He who chastens is a Father.

etymology: From un-, not, and prepared, from Latin praeparare, to make ready beforehand, from prae, before, and parare, to make ready. Paul's Greek means not ready.
biblical_def: Paul had been gathering a collection for the poor saints in Jerusalem. He had boasted to the Macedonians that Achaia was ready a year before, and their zeal had stirred the Macedonians to give beyond their power. Now he sends brethren ahead to Corinth, “Lest haply if they of Macedonia come with me, and find you unprepared, we (that we say not, ye) should be ashamed in this same confident boasting.” Paul wants the gift ready, “as a matter of bounty, and not as of covetousness” (2 Corinthians 9:5), so that it would not be squeezed out at the last moment under pressure. The principle is that giving should be planned and willing, not hasty and grudging: “Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver” (9:7). Paul's concern for being found unprepared also reflects his care for the church's testimony before other churches. Behind it all stands the motive he names at the end: “Thanks be unto God for his unspeakable gift” (9:15).

corruption_summary: Christian giving is either reduced to pressured, last-minute appeals or inflated by prosperity teaching into an investment that obliges God to repay with wealth.
corruption_paragraphs: Two errors distort giving. One is the high-pressure appeal that extracts gifts by emotion or guilt at the last moment, the very thing Paul sought to avoid. The other is the prosperity gospel, which turns 2 Corinthians 9:6 into a formula: sow money to reap money.

Paul's pattern is planned, willing, cheerful giving, motivated by God's unspeakable gift in Christ and aimed at the relief of the saints and the glory of God. The sowing and reaping he speaks of is a harvest of righteousness and thanksgiving, not personal enrichment.
